en: The Dharani of the Most Victorious Mind for Fulfilling All Wishes of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha;
The Method for Seeking the Retention of What is Heard,
from the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, Chapter on the Accomplishment of All Meanings.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the Bhagavat entered the samādhi of the equality of all pāramitās.
Having arisen from meditative concentration, he then spoke this most supreme heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-dhāraṇī*) of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, which fulfills all vows, saying:
*Namo ākāśaparyaye oṃ ari karmari muri svāhā.* The Blessed One said: "Bhagavān."
This dhāraṇī has been spoken by all Buddhas of the past and present alike.
If one can constantly recite this dhāraṇī, [one shall attain...]
All karmic obstructions, including the five crimes of immediate retribution committed since beginningless time, shall be completely extinguished.
One will constantly receive the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Until they attain Buddhahood,
the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha will constantly follow and protect them in every place where they are born.
May all sentient beings always delight in beholding [them],
may all their virtuous aspirations be fulfilled without exception,
and may all their sufferings and afflictions be entirely eliminated.
One will always be reborn among humans or devas and never fall into the evil realms.
In every place of birth, one will constantly remember past lives.
Even without performing further ritual practices, merely being able to recite this constantly brings forth such merit.
If one wishes to apply dhāraṇī-mantra recitation to this dhāraṇī in order to seek the power of hearing and retaining,
one should first draw a full moon upon silk, white cotton cloth, or a clean wooden board.
Within this, one should paint an image of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha;
its size should be no less than one cubit,
or even greater, as far as one's ability permits.
The Bodhisattva’s full moon-like face is proportionate to its waxing and waning;
his body is golden in color,
and he sits with his right half-lotus foot raised upon a precious lotus flower.
The right hand suppresses the left.
His countenance is exceptionally sublime, manifesting an expression of serene joy and delight.
Upon his jeweled crown are five Buddha images.
Seated in the full lotus posture,
the Bodhisattva holds a white lotus flower in his left hand,
which has a slight reddish hue.
Upon the flower pedestal is a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) of vaidūrya color,
emitting blazing yellow light;
his right hand further forms the mudrā for granting all boons.
With the five fingers hanging down and the palms facing outward,
this is the *varada-mudrā*.
Once the painted image has been completed:
One should place the image in a secluded and tranquil location,
such as a clean room, a stupa, a temple, a mountain peak, or beneath a tree,
settling it in whichever spot is appropriate.
Face directly west, or allow it to face north;
cover it with clean objects and construct a square wooden maṇḍala beneath it.
It should reach one cubit (hasta), or more than that as desired;
beneath the altar, four legs should be installed,
or it may be supported by a woven frame.
The distance from the top to the ground should be exactly four finger-widths.
Regarding the boards, it is most excellent if they are made of sandalwood or aloeswood;
otherwise, one may also use cypress or other fragrant woods.
Having performed the ritual according to the Dharma, place it before the image.
Next, one should carefully prepare the five kinds of offerings, namely:
unguents, various flowers, incense, food and drink, and lamps.
As for the fragrant ointment, grind white sandalwood to prepare it.
As for the flowers, use those produced from seasonal medicinal herbs;
if there are no seasonal flowers, one should use non-glutinous rice instead.
One may burn buckwheat, or take the leaves of tangerine, cypress, and so forth;
or use cloves to serve as flower offerings.
For incense, one should simply use aloeswood, sandalwood, or camphor according to what is appropriate for the occasion.
Regarding food, one must always ensure it is fresh and pure to eliminate foul odors;
as for lamps, cow’s ghee is permitted as well.
When one is about to prepare these items:
One must wash the hands and face at dawn, maintain ritual purity according to the dharma,
and having fully prepared everything,
place it at the edge of the mandala.
Thereafter, he goes outside and washes his hands again with pure water.
He then forms a mudrā, holding the palms together to receive the pure water.
Recite the dhāraṇī three times and then drink it immediately.
As for the hand gesture (*mudrā*):
first, extend the five fingers of the right hand upward with the palm facing up.
Bend the index finger and the thumb so that they touch each other,
forming a shape like one pinching incense.
This is the Seal of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva for Accomplishing All Deeds.
Again, using this mudrā as before to receive the water,
once the recitation of the dhāraṇī has been completed three times,
sprinkle it upon the crown of the head and the body.
Immediately, one should cause everything both inside and outside to be completely purified.
Next, one should proceed to the place where the image is located;
with a sincere heart, one should prostrate and sit facing the Bodhisattva in the half-lotus position.
Lift away the covering from atop the image.
Next, one must perform the *rakṣāhasta-mudrā* (the hand-seal of the protective hand).
As for the characteristics of this mudrā:
First raise the right hand,
then join the index finger and the thumb together,
forming a shape as if holding incense.
Bend the second joint of the index finger,
ensuring that its first joint is perfectly straight;
only then does it constitute the seal-form.
Having performed this mudrā according to the Dharma,
place it upon the crown of the head and recite the dhāraṇī once;
next, place it on the right shoulder and recite it once again.
The same is done for the heart and throat on the left shoulder.
Having performed this rite for protecting the body,
all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha [will protect you].
By taking this person under their protection,
all karmic obstacles will be completely extinguished;
body and mind will become pure, and merit and wisdom will increase.
None of the māras or vināyakas shall find an opportunity.
Again, form the previous mudrā with the palms supporting pure water and recite the dhāraṇī once.
Sprinkle the various offering substances, such as the scented unguents, upon the altar and the ground surrounding it.
Then, once again perform the hand-seal for protecting the body as before;
place it over the scented unguents and recite the dhāraṇī once.
For all other items, such as flowers and incense, up to wooden altars,
one should perform this rite in the same manner for each; once this method has been performed,
the flowers, incense, and other objects will immediately become pure.
Again, perform the hand-seal of protecting the body,
circling it three times to the right while moving the fingers up and down;
merely move the seal without shaking the body and recite the dhāraṇī seven times.
According to the distance and extent of one's own mind,
one should demarcate the realms of the ten directions;
next, one should close the eyes and engage in contemplation.
The true body of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is equal to this image and no different from it.
Furthermore, employing the protection-of-the-body mudrā and forming the mental visualization,
one invites the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Having recited the dhāraṇī twenty-five times,
one immediately raises the index finger and beckons inward once,
then returns the index finger to its original position.
Furthermore, form this mudrā and recite the dhāraṇī three times.
Use the lotus upon the cloth as a seat,
and further visualize the Bodhisattva coming to sit upon this flower.
Even upon opening one's eyes and seeing the Bodhisattva,
one should give rise to a sense of wonder and understand this to be the true body.
Furthermore, recite [the mantra] three times, perform the hand gestures as before, and reflect thus:
The Bodhisattva has now arrived here.
This power of the dhāraṇī is beyond my capability.
I only pray that the Venerable One will remain here for a while.
Next, take the unguent and recite the dhāraṇī once;
use it to smear the maṇḍala.
Then, again take flowers and recite [the dhāraṇī] once more, scattering them upon the maṇḍala.
One should take the incense, food and drink, and lamps in succession,
reciting [the mantra] once for each while holding them as an offering.
Having placed them at the edge of the altar, one should further reflect thus:
All these banners, canopies, pure incense, flowers, and various precious articles are produced through the cultivation of the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
they are entirely magnificent and exquisite.
Furthermore, form the hand-seal and recite the dhāraṇī once.
Visualize as before,
and all articles of offering will be fully prepared.
One should then take these and offer them to all Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas;
such an application of the mind is the supreme among all forms of offering.
Should one be unable to provide offerings of ointments and the like, [one should instead apply the mind in this way].
It suffices to perform the second mental visualization for the offering;
the practice will likewise be accomplished.
Then, using the mudrā, one should count the beads.
Recite the dhāraṇī while clearly keeping track of the number of recitations;
when reciting, close your eyes and visualize a full moon upon the heart of the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the syllables of the dhāraṇī being recited all appear within the full moon as golden in color;
these syllables then flow forth from that full moon.
The water poured down upon the crowns of the practitioners' heads;
it then entered their mouths and emerged from them, flowing into the feet of the Bodhisattva as if speaking words of its own accord to address the Bodhisattva’s feet.
This continued until the recitation of the dhāraṇī had not yet ceased.
The characters being contemplated revolve and circulate in succession without interruption, turning like a wheel;
if body and mind become weary, one must then cease.
With utmost sincerity, gaze upon him, then sit and prostrate.
Close your eyes and again visualize the Bodhisattva Full Moon;
once you have visualized him with extreme clarity, [proceed].
One should further direct the mind so that it gradually increases until it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; then,
one should again gradually narrow the visualization until,
at the final stage, its extent is as it was originally.
Only then does one emerge from the visualization.
Again, having performed the aforementioned hand-seal and recited the dhāraṇī three times,
one raises the thumb to bid farewell to the bodhisattva.
Form this thought: "I pray that you will grant your compassion, bestow your gifts, and rejoice.
May you deign to descend again for future dharma assemblies.
Recite the dhāraṇī in this manner.
According to one's capacity, one may ascend once a day or twice a day;
from beginning to end, it should be done as on the first day.
The number of recitations, whether more or less, shall also be as stated above;
it must not be increased or decreased.
Calculating the total for both the preceding and subsequent sections, they must reach one million recitations.
The number of recitations is thus completed, though there is no fixed time limit;
however, during the interval, no gaps or omissions are permitted.
Subsequently, on the occasion of a solar or lunar eclipse, one should perform them.
According to one's capacity, one should give away food, drink,
and material wealth to make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Then, one should move the Bodhisattva image and the altar to a clean, open space.
Having established [the image],
take one *liang* of cow’s ghee and place it within a vessel of refined copper.
Furthermore, take seven leaves and one branch from a milky-sap tree and place them at the edge of the altar;
increase the number of flowers, incense, and other offerings by several times their usual amount.
The methods for making offerings are each the same as before.
Having completed the offerings,
take the aforementioned tree leaves and spread them again upon the altar.
Furthermore, place a vessel of clarified butter upon a leaf;
again, forming the mudrā, recite the dhāraṇī three times to protect this clarified butter.
Furthermore, stir the clarified butter with a tree branch;
do not let your hand rest.
Keep your eyes fixed on the sun and moon, while also watching the butter.
Recite the dhāraṇī an unlimited number of times.
From the beginning of the eclipse until it has receded and the moon is no longer obscured,
three signs will appear within that ghee.
First is vapor;
second is smoke;
third is fire.
Among these three grades— lower, middling, and superior—
whichever single quality one attains, the rite is accomplished.
Once this sign has been obtained, it immediately becomes a divine medicine.
If one consumes this medicine, one will immediately attain the power of hearing and retaining;
whatever passes through the ears or eyes, both the text and its meaning will be understood,
and it will be recorded in the mind so that there is never any forgetfulness.
The remaining benefits are immeasurable and boundless;
for now, I shall briefly describe a small portion of these merits,
from the point of reaching the stage of "reversing retreat" up until its perfection.
If the three characteristics are not accomplished because the dharmas are absent,
one should again begin from the very beginning and perform it up to seven times.
Even if one has committed the five heinous crimes or other extremely grave karmic obstructions, they shall all be extinguished;
this dharma-gate is definitively accomplished.
This is the *Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Mind for Fulfilling All Wishes* of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, and the method for seeking the power of hearing and retaining.
